positions.source_passage: I recommend in my opinion that AI should never be used without human oversight, AI therapists that purport to treat psychiatric conditions be regulated by the FDA, and that AI device manufacturers must prove a minimum standard of accuracy before approval. Post-market review is not enough when AI is such a new technology with many unknowns.
positions.position_gist: Opposes accepting greater premarket uncertainty in exchange for postmarket monitoring, arguing manufacturers must demonstrate a minimum standard of accuracy before approval because postmarket review alone is insufficient for such a new technology.

positions.source_passage: My comment primarily pertains to question 18. AI is a software that relies on training data, and sometime data can be out of context of inaccurate.  For example, there was a case involving a man who asked ChatGPT to eliminate sodium chloride from his diet. The AI used data on bromide-chloride substitution for other purposes and suggested bromide. The man started consuming bromide instead of salt and ended up in hospital. This suggests severe risks when it comes to AI for information without doctor oversight.
positions.position_gist: Argues, using the ChatGPT bromide poisoning case, that GenAI delivering health information directly to users without clinician oversight poses severe risk because training data can be applied out of context.

positions.source_passage: while I am unsure whether this falls into the scope of the discussion, AI therapists for psychiatric conditions are an issue that should also be evaluated. In a report by Common Sense Media, where a tester acted as a teen with bulimia nervosa talking to Wysa and among other things, Wysa encouraged weight loss and ignored a description of Russellply for some AI therapists, particularly those who claim to treat psychiatric conditions to be regulated similarly to medical devices to mitigate these risks.
positions.position_gist: Recommends (with acknowledged uncertainty about scope) that consumer-facing AI 'therapist' products claiming to treat psychiatric conditions be regulated similarly to medical devices, citing a documented failure to recognize eating-disorder signs in a patient-facing chatbot.

positions.source_passage: AI’s propensity to hallucinate is not limited to chatbot dialogue. A report by Reuters state that an AI ignored abnormal heartbeats and misidentified body parts of a foetus. Should AI be relied on for diagnosis, serious conditions could be missed or misdiagnosed.
positions.position_gist: Cites reported diagnostic-imaging errors (missed arrhythmias, misidentified fetal anatomy) as evidence that hallucination risk extends beyond chatbots and that reliance on AI for diagnosis could cause missed or incorrect diagnoses.

positions.source_passage: Therefore, I recommend in my opinion that AI should never be used without human oversight
positions.position_gist: Recommends that GenAI-enabled devices never operate without human oversight.
